extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners, patent prosecutors, and patent attorneys (patent practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining when a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (means- or step-plus-function), and for assessing whether the specification discloses corresponding structure/material/acts (including computer-implemented algorithms) sufficient to support such limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: When 35 U.S.C. 112(f) applies (invocation trigger)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners will apply 35 U.S.C. 112(f) to a claim limitation that uses the term 'means' or generic placeholder associated with functional language, unless that term is (1) preceded by a structural modifier, defined in the specification as a particular structure or known by one skilled in the art, that denotes the type of structural device (e.g., 'filters'), or (2) otherwise modified by sufficient structure or material for achieving the claimed function. Similarly, examiners will apply 35 U.S.C. 112(f) to a claim limitation that uses the term 'step for' unless that term is modified by sufficient acts for performing the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and case law: generic placeholders like 'mechanism,' 'element,' 'member' coupled with a function typically invoke 112(f) absent structural meaning (Massachusetts Inst. of Tech., Williamson). A generic placeholder preceded by a structural modifier (e.g., 'detent mechanism') may avoid 112(f) where the modifier denotes a type of structural device understood in the art (Greenberg).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural modifier exception
rubrics_metrics.description: A limitation will not invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) if there is a structural modifier that further describes the term 'means' or the generic placeholder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, a generic placeholder like 'mechanism' standing alone may invoke 112(f) when coupled with a function, but it will not invoke 112(f) when it is preceded by a structural modifier (e.g., 'detent mechanism') if that modifier denotes a generally understood structural device (Greenberg, 91 F.3d at 1583). By contrast, non-structural modifiers (e.g., 'colorant selection mechanism') that lack an art-recognized structural meaning will not avoid 112(f) (Massachusetts Inst. of Tech.).

rubrics_metrics.name: How to determine whether a modifier denotes structure
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether a word, term, or phrase coupled with a function denotes structure, examiners may check whether: (1) the specification provides a description sufficient to inform one of ordinary skill in the art that the term denotes structure; (2) general and subject matter specific dictionaries provide evidence that the term has achieved recognition as a noun denoting structure; and/or (3) the prior art provides evidence that the term is an art-recognized structure to perform the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an evidentiary, fact-based inquiry (Ex parte Rodriguez, precedential). Use specification disclosure, dictionaries, and prior art to assess whether the modifier imparts structural significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant can rebut presumption of invocation
rubrics_metrics.description: During examination, applicants have the opportunity and the obligation to define their inventions precisely, including whether a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f). If the term 'means' or 'step' or a generic placeholder is modified by sufficient structure, material or acts for achieving the specified function, the USPTO will consider that presumption has been rebutted and will not apply 35 U.S.C. 112(f) until such modifying language is deleted from the claim limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should include structure/material/acts in the claim language or clarify in specification/arguments to rebut the means-plus-function presumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element-by-element analysis required
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary to decide on an element by element basis whether 35 U.S.C. 112(f) applies. Each claim must be independently reviewed to determine the applicability of 35 U.S.C. 112(f) even where the application contains substantially similar process and apparatus claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer that a limitation in a claim is governed by 112(f) merely because similar language appears in another claim that invokes 112(f) (O.I. Corp., IMS Technology). Interpret each limitation based on its own language and the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corresponding-structure disclosure requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The corresponding structure (or material or acts) of a means- (or step-) plus-function limitation must be disclosed in the specification itself in a way that one skilled in the art will understand what structure (or material or acts) will perform the recited function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is no disclosure of structure, material or acts for performing the recited function, the claim fails to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112(b). Disclosure may be explicit, implicit/inherent, or in drawings if it would have been clear to those skilled in the art (Atmel; Dossel; Vas-Cath). A bare statement that known techniques can be used does not disclose structure (Biomedino).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invocation of 112(f) does not relieve 112(a)/(b) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The invocation of 35 U.S.C. 112(f) does not exempt an applicant from compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA first and second paragraphs). Means-plus-function language can be used in the claims, but the claims must still accurately define the invention and the specification must meet written description and enablement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess written description and enablement separately; structure disclosure for 112(f) is closely related to written description/enablement issues (Donaldson, In re Knowlton, Aristocrat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-implemented means-plus-function: algorithm disclosure required
rubrics_metrics.description: For a computer-implemented 35 U.S.C. 112(f) claim limitation, the specification must disclose an algorithm for performing the claimed specific computer function, or else the claim is indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the disclosed structure is a computer programmed to carry out an algorithm, the disclosed structure is that special-purpose computer programmed to perform the disclosed algorithm, not merely a general purpose computer (Net MoneyIN, In re Aoyama, WMS Gaming, Aristocrat).

rubrics_metrics.name: General purpose computer alone is insufficient (except for basic coextensive functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The corresponding structure is not simply a general purpose computer by itself but the special purpose computer as programmed to perform the disclosed algorithm. A microprocessor or general purpose computer lends sufficient structure only to basic functions coextensive with a microprocessor (e.g., 'receiving,' 'storing,' 'processing' data). All other computer-implemented functions require disclosure of an algorithm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EON Corp. and Katz: a microprocessor suffices only where the claimed function is coextensive with the microprocessor itself. 'Special programming' includes any functionality not coextensive with a general-purpose computer (EON Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and sufficiency of an algorithm disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: An algorithm may be expressed in any understandable terms including as a mathematical formula, in prose, in a flow chart, or in any other manner that provides sufficient structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sufficiency of the algorithm is determined in view of what one of ordinary skill in the art would understand as sufficient to define the structure and make the boundaries of the claim understandable. The examiner should determine whether one skilled in the art would know how to program the computer to perform the necessary steps (Aristocrat, Finisar, Intel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple functions require disclosure for all functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a means-plus-function limitation performs multiple identifiable functions, the specification must disclose adequate corresponding structure (or algorithm) to perform all of the claimed functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification discloses an algorithm that only accomplishes one of multiple functions, the limitation is treated as if no algorithm were disclosed (Noah, Williamson, Media Rights Technologies). Case examples found claims indefinite where structure/algorithm for certain functions (e.g., 'coordinating' or 'diverting a data pathway') were not disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency indicators (black box/abstract outcome descriptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere reference to a general purpose computer with appropriate programming without providing an explanation of the appropriate programming, or simply reciting 'software' without providing detail about the means to accomplish a specific software function, will not be an adequate disclosure of the corresponding structure to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References to undefined components (e.g., 'access control manager'), 'logic,' 'code,' or other black-box abstractions are insufficient (Blackboard, Net MoneyIN, Ex parte Rodriguez). Also, mere outcome descriptions (describing what the function achieves) rather than how it is performed are inadequate (Aristocrat, Blackboard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of failing to disclose corresponding structure/algorithm
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification explicitly discloses no corresponding algorithm (for computer-implemented limitations) or otherwise fails to disclose corresponding structure/material/acts for the claimed function, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA second paragraph) is appropriate and the claim may be indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit precedent upholds invalidity where no operative algorithm or corresponding structure is disclosed (Advanced Ground Information Systems v. Life360; Blackboard; Media Rights; Noah). The examiner should reject as indefinite when disclosure is lacking.
